objective: T-20260930-03: do US year-to-date losers (ADV top 1,500, close >= 5 USD, funds excluded) bought at the open after 15 December and held to 15 or 31 January beat the equal-weight pool after ADV-tiered costs in ten December windows 2016-2025, by at least 1.5 percent, in at least 7 of 10 years, year-clustered t >= 2, with the February and June placebo windows summing to at most half, and both Dec 2024 and Dec 2025 positive?

sources.core_claim: Ivkovic, Poterba and Weisbenner (NBER w10275, January 2004) compare a large discount broker's individual-investor trades in taxable versus tax-deferred accounts and find tax-loss selling throughout the calendar year, most pronounced in December and especially for investors who realized capital gains elsewhere in the portfolio, plus a capital-gains lock-in effect.
sources.project_applicability: Establishes that December selling of losers by taxable individuals exists; motivates the mid-December entry.
sources.reflection: Trade-level evidence only; gives no stock-price return size for a December-to-January rebound, and covers the 1990s before the growth of tax-sheltered accounts.

sources.core_claim: Grinblatt and Keloharju (draft 2002-07-03, NBER w8745) find that Finnish investors realize losses more than gains toward the end of December and repurchase the sold stocks, producing net tax-loss buying pressure that is negative before the turn of the year and positive afterwards, and that turn-of-the-year returns, particularly for small firms, relate to that pressure.
sources.project_applicability: Supports the sign of the price pressure (December negative, January positive) that the mid-December entry tries to harvest.
sources.reflection: Finnish market with a different tax regime; 1990s sample; regression evidence, no tradeable long-only excess return net of costs.

sources.core_claim: Schwert (NBER w9277) shows on CRSP data that the small-minus-large NYSE return difference in the first 15 calendar days of January was still reliably positive after publication (daily alpha 0.00641, t 9.87, 1962-2001; 0.00565, t 5.37, 1990-2001), while the small-firm premium overall was much smaller after 1982 than in 1926-1982.
sources.project_applicability: Shows the turn-of-the-year window effect survived publication through 2001 for the small-minus-large spread; ends 2001, so it says nothing about 2016-2026.
sources.reflection: Size spread, not year-to-date losers; ends in 2001; the fading after 2001 is not measured.

sources.core_claim: Kaul, Mehrotra, Morck and Phillips (EFMA 2025 working paper) document a 3.1 percent January price increase in NYSE stocks over 1874-1917, before income taxes, and find larger January returns for small stocks, stocks with capital losses, illiquid stocks and volatile stocks, pointing to arbitrage costs as the reason the effect persists.
sources.project_applicability: Supports that losers and illiquid stocks carry the larger January return, and argues against pure tax explanation; so the pool restriction to ADV top 1,500 may remove the illiquid stocks where the effect is largest.
sources.reflection: Historic sample before income taxes and modern institutions; not a 2016-2026 estimate; working-paper draft.

sources.core_claim: McLean and Pontiff (October 2012 working-paper version of the JF 2016 article) study 82 published return predictors and find that the average post-publication decay, attributed to both statistical bias and price pressure from aware investors, is about 35 percent, larger for anomaly portfolios of large, liquid stocks.
sources.project_applicability: Prior that a 1983-era calendar anomaly is weaker in 2016-2025 and weaker in liquid stocks; sets the low prior stated in the queue.
sources.reflection: Average across 82 characteristics; the January-loser effect is not singled out.

sources.core_claim: Anderson, Gerlach and DiTraglia (William and Mary WP 15, March 2005) find in two laboratory auction environments that prices in the January markets were systematically higher than those in December, suggesting a psychological contribution to the January effect.
sources.project_applicability: Weak side evidence that a January-over-December price gap can arise without taxes.
sources.reflection: Lab experiment; no market data; no return size for a stock strategy.

sources.core_claim: Quantpedia's January Effect in Stocks page describes the rule 'invest in small-cap stocks at the beginning of each January, stay invested in large-cap stocks for the rest of the year' with indicative 12.7 percent per annum on 1947-2007 source-paper data (Easterday, Sen, Stephan), and states the strategy is long-only equity factor exposure, not a hedge.
sources.project_applicability: Existing practitioner packaging of the calendar effect is a size tilt, not a loser tilt, and its published numbers end in 2007.
sources.reflection: Aggregator page summarizing an SSRN paper; no post-2007 numbers; not a loser-selection rule.

sources.core_claim: Globe and Mail (2025-12-11), search summary only, body paywalled: TSX stocks down more than 15 percent year to date underperform by nearly 4 percent from mid-November to mid-December and outperform by 3.6 percent from mid-December to mid-January.
sources.project_applicability: Low prior: no US post-2015 effect size in any opened source.
sources.reflection: Paywall; Canadian sample; practitioner summary; not opened, so not used as an effect size.

sources.core_claim: JFIR 'Tax-loss selling and the January effect revisited', search snippet only (HTTP 403 on fetch): reports the January effect fading, likely because of more tax-sheltered accounts.
sources.project_applicability: Low prior: no US post-2015 effect size in any opened source.
